raw.text:
CTO role: expand a profitable SaaS into Data & Insights ($600k ARR, 10% equity), Remote & Solo I am looking for a CTO to take our profitable B2B SaaS into its next chapter.

You will be the sole engineer in charge of the company, with a 10% equity stake. We are a bootstrapped SaaS with $600k ARR and $250k profit with 1,600 customers.

We build tools to help businesses that sell on a large European e-commerce platform, similar to Amazon. Our users rate us with 4.9 out of 5 stars on Google. After 6 years as the founder, I will step back. You will be the sole engineer: no team, no designer, you build it. You get ownership with a 10% equity stake. With ownership comes full responsibility. If something breaks at 9pm, you get an alert and you fix it at 9pm. Even on a holiday. Hence, this job is not for everyone.

We have become a successful SaaS through our automations: such as invoicing and emailing. Our software has processed more than 100M orders worth $4B in revenue. Hundreds of sellers use our tools every day. These features stay as they are, and they must keep working.

Our next chapter, that you will build out, is on data and insights. A seller can vibecode an automation, but nobody can vibecode a dataset. We have a huge database and many platform API keys. This is our moat. You turn numbers into simple, beautiful tools that make sellers’ lives easier. You talk to customers to find out what they need. Don’t worry - I will help you land and I have a roadmap in mind. We also have competitors to take inspiration from. Just don’t expect a design you only have to implement. You design too.

I have been running the place for the past 6 years, and now I want to do something different. I will step out of the day to day. From time to time I will check in with you to decide our roadmap together. Your team consists of an experienced customer support guy. During the week, he brings you some questions that need your technical answer. We have a Systems Administrator that manages our servers.

You are the one-man-army, you take pride in high-quality products, and you want the responsibility that comes with them. This is a role for a senior full-stack engineer with 8+ years of experience. You have been responsible for production systems. You have built and released complete features with little or no outside help. If you have not yet owned a live product from end to end, this role comes too early for you. Coding agents make it easier than ever to write code. That lets us build faster and better, but it also invites bloat and slop. Our codebase has been carefully crafted over many years, and you continue to handle it with the care it deserves.

Current stack - React, TypeScript - Python, Pyramid - Postgres, SQLAlchemy

Details - Salary: €80k - €150k a year (before all taxes) - Equity: 10% after 1 year, with the opportunity to grow further - Fully remote - European or American timezone - Fluent English

Interested? Send me an email on jamecroon@protonmail.com (anon mailbox for confidentiality)

title: Launch HN: StarSling (YC P25) – Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos
author: yonasb

raw.text:
We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling (https://starsling.dev), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows.

Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost.

Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762.

I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill.

We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww.

Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry - Propose an optimization - Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change - Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant - Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence

We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time: - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x)

Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills. The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself.

We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly (https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks).

We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks.

To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start. You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes.

Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge.

We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!

title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
author: sanchitmonga22

raw.text:
Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :)

What it does today:

- Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router.

- Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks.

- Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance.

We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results.

But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now.

We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions:

- 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency)

-The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps.

Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels.

So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8.

The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within

There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections.

You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results:

https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega...

Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback.

Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai.

We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.
raw.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium

title: Ask HN: Anyone else blurting?
author: l33tbro

raw.text:
Like most, I was stoked on LLMs when they became available. Particularly on the earlier free tiers where the slightly questionable answers were offset by generous tokens.

Now, I'm finding that having to use this tech is becoming much less fun. The constant corrections, the constant prompting for greater brevity, the grating certainty and sycophancy.

Others probably are forgiving considering the net benefit. But for me it honestly now feels like a chore, which is reflected in how my frustration is now appearing in how I communicate to it now.

Instead of articulating and making my prompts precise, I'm just straight-out blurting. Typos, missed words, poor semantic structure - I guess I maybe at some point reasoned that "it will get the picture, so why waste effort being articulate?" Or maybe I'm just anticipating that it is going to get it 15 percent wrong, so why even try and be articulate. Just blurt and steer. Blurt and steer.

Is anyone else finding this? I actually sometimes worry about it. I feel it's not just the fact that I'm offloading my cognition to it that is making me dumber, it is the way I'm communicating with it. They say the act of writing is tied to the act of thinking, and my prompts are basicslly the typographic equivalent of grunting right now.

title: Show HN: Belay – formal verification for SQLite migrations and queries in Lean 4
author: neprotivo

raw.text:
Hi, I'm Tzanko and I'm the author of Belay.

Belay is a Lean 4 library for doing formal verification of SQLite queries and migrations. It implements a semantic model of a subset of SQLite, validated by differential tests that compare the output against native SQLite.

With Belay I wanted to see how difficult it is to use formal verification for everyday development tasks. It turns out it can be made not much harder than writing an integration test: you state the claim, the agent writes the proof, and Lean's kernel checks it, so the only thing you have to read is the claim (longer write-up on the motivation and agent workflow: https://vihren.dev/blog/20261112-belay/).

While a migration is being written, your agent can run #sql_check, which searches small databases for counterexamples to a claim, and is as easy to run as a linter.

Once the migration is settled, the agent writes a proof of the claims you need, for example that the migration preserves the results of existing queries and succeeds on valid data.

Currently Belay supports a subset of SQLite 3.51.0, cross-checked against native SQLite on 5,768 differential test cases, most of which come from SQLite's own test suite. Unsupported SQL is rejected with a reason and never approximated. Not every rule of the model has had a human audit yet. The model covers single-connection operational semantics only: it says nothing about query plans, locks, concurrency or crash behavior.

I think this approach can make formal verification as routine as testing, though two things stand in the way. The first is coverage: the model has to cover the full semantics of SQLite and all of its recent versions, and the same work has to be done for other engines such as PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. The second is proof cost: the proofs of common claims are still long for the agent to write, and they have to become short. I'm looking for design partners who want this for their workloads on SQLite or other open-source databases, because a real workload is the best guide to what to cover first. The models that come out of that work become part of Belay as open source. Reach out at contact@vihren.dev.

If you know a tricky SQLite edge case where the model might diverge from native SQLite, or a gnarly migration bug you've hit in production, I'd love to test it and hear your thoughts.

title: Show HN: Open-source multi-player artifacts that update themselves
author: ajuhasz

raw.text:
Rally is a multi-player platform to build reactive micro-applications together that connects event streams to agents that then update the artifact. We've had pilots build a PR dashboard that sorts by risk assessment (an agent actually reads the code) per PR, a micro-CRM that pulls in live deals from multiple Gmail inboxes, and a shared grocery list that groups items by store aisle.

We're similar to Muse's Spaces, Google's TableTop, and the standard artifacts most harnesses now support. Our differentiator is being multi-player so groups can iterate together, artifacts calling agents on incoming events so updates can be more sophisticated than an API call, and giving artifacts a full application stack.

Under the hood, each artifact is a Cloudflare Durable Object with its own SQLite database, compute, and storage.

As an example this is our podcast artifact that helps us keep up-to-date on what happened on the repo each day https://connected-tidy-crystalline-haldane-g.rallyuserconten...

GitHub: https://github.com/juno-ai-labs/avalon

title: Ask HN: UK Equivalent for Power Switch Tail/IoT Power Relay?
author: a2fz

raw.text:
Basically I just want a 230 volt relay that I can turn on/off with a Raspberry Pi/Ardunio, but I don't feel confident enough to tinker with mains electricity myself. I saw the Powerswitch tail 2 (https://www.adafruit.com/product/268) a while ago, which has been discontinued but replaced with the IoT Power Relay (https://www.adafruit.com/product/2935). Both look great, the problem is that they're only made for US plugs at American voltage and I want something I can use with a UK plug. Anyone know of anything for this?

I have a few Wi-Fi smart plugs but I'd like something simple that I can hardwire and control myself without any wireless connectivity. Just a pre-made relay cable. This feels like something I should be able to easily find online but I guess I'm just bad at googling?
